>ends. The blocking vampire wants to play Majesty, then pay a blood to
>untap. Is this legal, or does combat end when the acting vampire chooses

it's legal. Each player has an opportunity to announce strikes, and
the "untap" effect happens when the card is played, as opposed to when
strikes resolve.

So both players choose strikes, pay a blood to untap, and THEN strikes
resolve and the "combat ends" takes effect.

>vampire, removing himself from the game. Does the Hostile Takeover

this fashion to attempt to screw someone else needs to be beaten with
a stick.

I don't have any specific card text or rules support for this guess.

"Combat Ends: This effect ends combat immediately. This type of strike
is always the first to resolve, even before a strike done with first
strike, and ends combat before other strikes can be resolved or any
damage dealt. Combat ends is effective at any range. Combat ends is
not affected by a dodge, since dodge only cancels effects that are
directed at the dodging minion."

What that means is that, when you enter Strike Resolution, combat ends
immediately. It doesn't end combat as soon as it is played, since
strikes *all* have a slight delay built in - from Choose Strike to
Strike Resolution.

You misunderstand. Effects of a card happen when the card is played.

Majesty's text: Strike: Combat Ends. (S) As above, and this vampire
may burn one blood to untap.

The "combat ends" strike resolves during the strike resolution phase.
The "burn one blood to untap" is not a side effect of ending combat;
it's an effect of playing the card. So when you play the card, during
the Choose Strike phase, you burn a blood and untap. Then, during the
Strike Resolution phase, combat ends.

This does mean that if you are the acting minion, you can play
Majesty, untap, and the reacting minion can play Wolf Claws and
Rotschreck, and you will be sent to torpor untapped, with your strike
never resolving.

Messages.Author: wes
Messages.Body:
I'm a bit confused by the animosity some players feel towards 'upstreamers'.

I imagine this topic has been covered in more detail before I arrived on the
scene, but nevertheless I don't see where this is coming from.

I regularly play a !Brujah deck. Mostly bruise and bleed but I also have
enough rush cards to threaten my predator should he need it. I have been
criticized by some players for doing exactly that. This makes no sense to
me.

There are two immediate strategies involved with playing and winning a game
of Jyhad. The first is ousting your prey. The second and most important is
NOT being ousted by your predator. If you are taking actions which
accomplish the latter, how is such criticism justified? Not that I am
playing JUST to win, but I would think that whatever I need to do to make my
deck survive a game should be acceptable within reason.

Now I understand that there is often a tactical disadvantage to weakening
your predator to the point that he is not a threat to his own predator, but
this only means that a balance must be struck. Similarly, if your predator
has more to worry about from his own predator than he has to gain from
attacking me, then that is an acceptable risk for me. As my focus stays on
surviving and ultimately winning the game, why is occasionally going
upstream considered bad playing?

The only instance I can think of that would qualify as playing badly is when
a deck is designed such that it has absolutely NO forward motion. In this
case, surviving a game may be possible but winning a game something else
entirely.

Cheers,
WES

That seems like a flawed way of looking at the game. I agree, not getting ousted
is important but I'm confused why you would make it, "the most important". I
actually don't think there's a way to reduce successful play down to prioritizing
_either_ not getting ousted over trying to oust your prey _or_ the reverse. The
truth is that you need to avoid being ousted long enough to give yourself a
reasonable chance of scoring victory points. But if avoiding being ousted is all
you try to do with little or no resources expended on offense, you'll inevitably
fail in your defense as well. Your prey can take a great deal of advantage of
not being attacked and use that to go around the circle and ultimately oust your
predator and then, despite your attention to defense, should be able to oust you
given the additional 12 or 18 blood he gained along with the victory points.

So ultimately, the best thing you can do to make your deck survive - if you count
surviving as being the last one out - is to pay a fair amount of attention to the
forward direction. Also, notice you can survive and still lose or tie even if
your prey goes 'round the whole circle but still loses to you.

I think the reason people get annoyed at a perceived lack of offense is that it
inevitably works to the advantage of the player's prey and often doesn't really work
to the advantage of that player much at all. If that's what's happening, you should
consider taking a look at what your overall strategy is actually gaining you. Do
you win with it regularly? If so, well, don't let us tell you anything. But if not,
then why cling to it so stubbornly?

> As my focus stays on
> surviving and ultimately winning the game, why is occasionally going
> upstream considered bad playing?

It isn't, if it's truly just "occasional". Especially with a combat deck,
this might be necessary. And if you play combat and your predator is a
stealth bleed or a vote deck that's successfully passing votes and you're
helpless to intercept, then you may be forced to oust your predator just
because it's all you can do with the board situation. It just depends on
what you mean by "occasionally going upstream".

Fred

A bruise-and-bleed deck needs to focus exactly that way; bleed

It's not. However, CONSTANTLY going upstream, such as Andrew referred
to in his message, is generally looked down on. Intercept decks that
never move forward and spend their time doing nothing but blocking
their predator are also filed in this category.

It's perfectly possible to ignore your prey and kill backwards, taking
advantage of the two-sided pressure available on your predator to get
each ousted rapidly, and then killing all of the final player's
vampires and ousting him to gain the final 2 VP, while theoretically 3
others players end up with 1 each and your original predator ends up
screwed.

It's not very likely to work, though; your initial prey will usually
gain a VP quickly due to the lack of forward pressure on him, and then
by the time you meet in the middle, it's possible that the additional
resources he's gained by ousting multiple prey will be enough to
overwhelm you in the endgame. More often than not, an "upstreamer"
will end up with 0 VP and be ousted BEFORE his original prey gets to
him. Worst-case scenario (fairly common, too); the original prey
sweeps through the other 3 players, leaving a score of 3 to 2 ... a
loss for the upstreamer, even though his plan worked almost perfectly.

>It's not. However, CONSTANTLY going upstream, such as Andrew referred

>to in his message, is generally looked down on. Intercept decks that
>never move forward and spend their time doing nothing but blocking
>their predator are also filed in this category.
>

CONSTANTLY doing anything deserves contempt as it reflects a lack of
flexibility, observation and intelligent play. Just as intercept
decks can block both predator and prey, upstream Rush decks can rush
whichever player needs rushing at the moment.

>It's perfectly possible to ignore your prey and kill backwards, taking
>advantage of the two-sided pressure available on your predator to get
>each ousted rapidly, and then killing all of the final player's
>vampires and ousting him to gain the final 2 VP, while theoretically 3
>others players end up with 1 each and your original predator ends up
>screwed.
>
>It's not very likely to work, though;

Probably not but it seems interesting to try for a while. The big
danger seems to be that your combat style must beat everyone else's.
Just one other deck at the table which trumps you (even if only
moderately well) and you're in trouble. During Thursday's descent
into Madness, my Bru/iBru sat between a pair of Gangrel and weren't
going anywhere in any direction.

>your initial prey will usually
>gain a VP quickly due to the lack of forward pressure on him

This you must stop - he's only allowed the VP from your (latest)
predator. This is a rush deck. It kills minions it doesn't like. If
it can't kill its prey's minions at will, it's not going forward in
any case.

>, and then
>by the time you meet in the middle, it's possible that the additional
>resources he's gained by ousting multiple prey will be enough to
>overwhelm you in the endgame.

Political Flux would address the new predator gets bigger problem, if
one could figure out how to get the vote passed.

>More often than not, an "upstreamer"
>will end up with 0 VP and be ousted BEFORE his original prey gets to
>him. Worst-case scenario (fairly common, too); the original prey
>sweeps through the other 3 players, leaving a score of 3 to 2 ... a
>loss for the upstreamer, even though his plan worked almost perfectly.

A loss but better than three other players.

Tom

you. It's just generally a better idea to focus closer to yourself

That's about right; I have no idea why my fingers typed those words.
It should read 'best REASONABLE case', too, since obviously the "best"
scenario involves you with 2 VP and everyone else with 1.

Worst case, actually, is running into a predator with piles of combat
defense and exploding gloriously in a "puff" of Potence.

Although I tend to prefer intercept-thuggy decks, the strategy ends up
being largely the same; except I generally attempt to slaughter BOTH
my prey and predator until I oust my first prey, and then immediately
turn my attention upstream. This gives me an extra VP and 6 pool
going into the final "head to head" confrontation; and allows me to
have a chance of winning the game 3 to 2.

One might ask why I don't just keep moving downstream. With an
intercept deck, you have a finite amount of Eagle's Sight. Those
generally get spent intercepting your prey's (D) actions, and you can
also intercept all his UNDIRECTED actions, so you can prevent him from
ever getting set up. You can't even stop your grandprey's UNDIRECTED
actions without Eagle's Sight, so you have no way to stop him from
making his deck at least START; although you can deliberately let your
prey bleed him a few times, lie, and say "Gosh, sorry, no Eagle's
Sight in hand. I'd love to help..." to make it a little easier.

So basically, after you maim your prey, you're going to be dealing
with a new deck in much better position. Since intercept decks'
weakness is usually in their bleed offense, it might be pointless to
attempt to bleed through him at the expense of your own defense; it's
safer to wait around and kill him when every dead minion on his part
is worth twice as much to you, and that initial VP ensures that you
can -force- a win as long as you can kill your grandprey at the last.

Of course, the BEST case scenario is that you oust your prey
approximately the same time your grandpredator ousts your predator;
and now you can intercept almost every action on the table, giving you
pretty solid control and good chances for a 4-1 run. =)

I know that if I want my deck to win, I can't really afford someone to
come cross-table and kill my most valuable minion just because he
thinks I'm getting too strong. If someone is capable of doing that
and inclined to do so, it behooves me to make sure that person is
GONE, so that I can sweep up the rest of the VPs on the table without
interference. After you Rush cross-table once, it won't be difficult
to convince the rest of the table that you're likely to do so again;
so you'll have 4 players against you, whereas if you confine yourself
to your prey/predator, you'll only have 2.

>In any case, how is the upstreamality supposed to come out of the
>closet? This is a rush deck which attacks some predator minions who
>look dangerous. The prey isn't highest priority though he gets some
>attention. This leads to a little extra pressure on grand-prey, while
>grand-predator gets a little extra help. If my predator gets ousted I
>don't shed any tears - is this what gives the game away?

You're missing the point. As soon as it becomes obvious that your
prey is not your highest priority, your deck will be marked as an
upstreamer. You will not likely get hassled SPECIFICALLY for that,
since most people will let well enough alone as long as they have some
benefit, but you might be surprised. Your grand-prey may well decide
"OK, if you aren't going to pressure my predator, then I'll just see
if I can oust you so as to get someone back there who WILL." And this
is, in fact, to his benefit. About the only two people who will leave
you alone will be your prey and your grand-predator... and if you're
actually Rushing your prey some, then he'll be against you too. And
you've said yourself that you might Rush your grand-predator to slow
HIM down... so much for HIS support.

>The only cross-table action I would expect to do is rushing
>grand-predator if he threatened an early oust? Why would anyone but
>him object to that? Surely many decks attempt to manipulate the table
>by delaying inconvenient ousts.

Many decks DO attempt to delay inconvenient ousts. Very few of them
do it by coming across and killing minions; the reason being that if
you have to kill someone cross-table, you must do it on YOUR turn,
which means that you may have to look at someone with 8 pool and say
"Uh oh, you're going to be ousted by the Toreador bleed machine next
turn"... and go kill a Toreador. It's not difficult for the victim to
sway the table into thinking of you as a loose cannon at that point,
since only you and the Toreador bleed deck knew that the oust was
coming soon; and even YOU are only guessing since you don't know his
hand.

Relying on waiting around until someone is obviously in dire straits
is not a good idea when you don't have a reactive deck. Eagle's
Sight, for example, can be saved until the actual bleed that would
oust someone hits the table, and THEN used. But a Rush deck has no
such luxury, and this puts a big target on its forehead when it tries
to manipulate tables, because it's using a sledgehammer instead of
just a wedge.

exclusively until you got down to the 1 on 1, where you should have
